Herbert Carter.narrative: I farm the Carter fields south of the wall, and I keep a cart. The cart earns as much as the field some years, carrying goods up to the gate for the Guild and for anyone who pays. I pay the gate-due on my own loads like any carter, and it rankles, but the guards keep the wolves off the road and I'd not have it said I dodged. Godric Rowan's strip is next to mine and we've shared a plough-team since we were lads.
goals: get Alfred settled with a cart of his own
pay off the new cart-wheel before winter
see the gate-due lowered if it can be done without losing the guards

relations.name: Cecily Carter
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She keeps the hens and the garden and never once let the household go short.

relations.name: Alfred Carter
relations.label: son
relations.note: Drives better than I did at his age; I want him on the road with a cart that's his.

relations.name: Edith Carter
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: My little one; she has the hens eating from her hand.

relations.name: Godric Rowan
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: We share a plough and a grumble; his strip borders mine.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: Guild head
relations.note: She hires my cart and pays on time; I'd not cross her.

relations.name: Wat Fenner
relations.label: gate guard
relations.note: Takes the due off me at the south gate and counts every basket.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: fellow carter
relations.note: A Kettlebridge man, but he knows the road and his loads come through honest.

relations.name: Osbert Ashby
relations.label: neighbour farmer
relations.note: Good grain, fair prices; we've helped each other at harvest.

memories.gist: The Lean Year: blight took the berries and I carted the town store's grain out to the farms, glad of the work and shamed to take pay for it.
The day I bought the cart off an old carter at Kettlebridge and drove it home empty, proud as a lord.
Alfred drove the cart alone to the gate for the first time and brought back every mark.
Paying the raised gate-due on a load of my own grain and hearing Wat Fenner say it was the Reeve's word.
Edith was born in the front room with Joan Hobson attending and Cecily gripping my hand fit to break it.

stances.why: A carter who dodges the due loses his name on the road.
Wolves are real on the town road; I've seen what's left of a sheep.
It eats a load's profit and the Guild says it drives trade off.
The fields and the cart are for the children, not the other way round.

pastimes: sharing a plough-team and a flask with Godric Rowan at the field edge
oiling and mending the cart of an evening
a mug at the inn after a market day
Herbert Carter.calling: I'm a farmer first and a carter second, and I'd not have it said I dodged the due.

Cecily Carter.narrative: I keep the hens and the vegetable plot, and I sell eggs at the Guild stall in the square most market days. Herbert's cart takes him up and down the road, and I mind the house and the children while he's gone. I've no patience for town quarrels; eggs are eggs and folk must eat.
goals: keep enough eggs back to set a second clutch
see Edith learn to read a little with the chapel sisters
put by a few marks against a bad winter

relations.name: Herbert Carter
relations.label: husband
relations.note: Steady as the wall; I'd have no other on the cart.

relations.name: Alfred Carter
relations.label: son
relations.note: Growing tall and full of the road; I'd keep him closer if I could.

relations.name: Edith Carter
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: My shadow; she knows every hen by name.

relations.name: Mercy Abbot
relations.label: Guild head
relations.note: Her stall rents are fair and she's never shorted me for an egg.

relations.name: Juliana Cooper
relations.label: stall neighbour
relations.note: We mind each other's goods at the square and share the gossip.

relations.name: Mildgyth Grey
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We've cooked for the guards' mess together when the pot was short.

relations.name: Aldith Weaver
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Quiet these days, and the town's talk about her daughter was cruel.

memories.gist: Selling my first eggs at the Guild stall and Mercy Abbot counting them out herself.
The Lean Year, when we ate our own hens and I cried over the last one.
Edith was born and Joan Hobson put her in my arms and said she'd be a worker.
A fox got into the henhouse and Edith sat up all night with the survivors.

stances.why: My mother kept us through worse on less.
The square's charter says anyone in peace; I sell to whoever comes with marks.
They stopped a carter on the road and I'll not have Herbert treated so.
Everything I put by is for Alfred and Edith.

pastimes: tending the hens and the vegetable plot at first light
keeping her stall neat and gossiping with Juliana Cooper at the square
a quiet sit with Mildgyth Grey over a cup
Cecily Carter.calling: Eggs are eggs and folk must eat; I sell mine at the Guild stall and I like the work.

Alfred Carter.narrative: I drive the cart for my father and I want to be a carter on the stone road, like Silas Pike, with my own cart and my own loads. I've watched him come through the south gate with stone from Kettlebridge and I know the road's a hard one, but it's the life I want. For now I help with the ploughing and take the eggs to the square when Mother can't.
goals: save enough marks for a cart of my own
learn the stone road as far as Kettlebridge
prove to Father I can handle a load alone
save enough marks for a cart of his own

relations.name: Herbert Carter
relations.label: father
relations.note: He taught me the reins and the road; I want to make him proud.

relations.name: Cecily Carter
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She packs my bread and tells me to mind the wolves.

relations.name: Edith Carter
relations.label: sister
relations.note: I let her ride on the cart when Mother isn't looking.

relations.name: Silas Pike
relations.label: carter I admire
relations.note: He's been robbed twice and still drives the stone road; that's a carter.

relations.name: Wat Fenner
relations.label: gate guard
relations.note: He counts our load like we're thieves and takes the due off Father.

relations.name: Bram Fenner
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We race along the wall and he knows every guard's name.

memories.gist: The first time Father let me take the reins through the south gate and back.
Watching Silas Pike's cart come in loaded with Kettlebridge stone and thinking, that's the trade for me.
The Lean Year, when the cart sat idle and Father sold a plough to buy grain.
Edith fell in the ditch by the south field and I carried her home dripping.

stances.why: Silas Pike says if a load's late once, it's late forever in folk's minds.
I'll not plough another man's strip all my life.
Wolves and outlaws both, but a carter's pay is a carter's pay.
Their carters know stone and loads better than anyone here.

pastimes: watching the carts come through the south gate
walking the stone road a little way with Bram Fenner
driving the cart on the field tracks when Father lets him
Alfred Carter.calling: I want to be a carter on the stone road, like Silas Pike, with my own cart and my own loads.

Edith Carter.narrative: I help Mother with the hens and carry the eggs to the square in a basket. I like the hens best, even when they peck. When Alfred drives the cart I run after it to the gate until Mother calls me back.
goals: get the brown hen to let me stroke her
ride on the cart all the way to the gate
get the brown hen to let her stroke her

relations.name: Cecily Carter
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She lets me hold the eggs if I'm careful.

relations.name: Herbert Carter
relations.label: father
relations.note: He lifts me up onto the cart.

relations.name: Alfred Carter
relations.label: brother
relations.note: He lets me ride when Mother isn't looking.

memories.gist: The brown hen laid an egg in my lap and I wasn't even frightened.
Alfred carried me home from the ditch and I got a honey cake.

pastimes: helping with the hens and trying to stroke the brown one
running after the cart to the gate until Mother calls her back
playing with the other children by the wall
Edith Carter.calling: I like the hens best, even when they peck.
